newsitem.title: USA: Regional jets key as pilots' board meets on offer.
newsitem.headline: Regional jets key as pilots' board meets on offer.

text.p: The issue of who will fly regional jets loomed again as a possible deal breaker Friday as the board of the Allied Pilots Association began discussing a new contract offer by American Airlines.

Even if the 18-member APA board backs the preliminary agreement reached Wednesday, it must still be ratified by the APA's 9,300 pilots, which proved a stumbling block to an earlier attempt to settle with American, the nation's No.2. carrier.
An accord reached last September got the backing of the board by 10-8, but 61 percent of the pilots turned it down in January.

"We do not expect any decision on the agreement in principle today," union spokesman Wally Pitts told reporters gathered at the hotel where the board was meeting. He said negotiators still had to put the offer into contract form.
Pitts emphasized that the question of whether Allied Pilots Association members would fly regional jets remained a key issue, although he declined to give any details.
"We're concerned American will expand the regional fleet and shrink the American fleet," he said.

There were reports that the Air Line Pilots Association, which represents pilots at American's regional operations, was due to meet with the APA to resolve the small jet issue. ALPA declined to comment and the APA said only that it was keeping ALPA informed about negotiations.
Union officials say the pilots are ready to strike on April 28 if no new agreement is reached.

The pilots briefly went on strike at midnight Feb. 14, but President Clinton immediately set up an emergency board, which sent the pilots back to work for 60 days while mediators drafted a proposed settlement.
During the period, American, a unit of AMR Corp., is also forbidden to engage in a lockout. But the carrier has said it would not try to operate without its staff pilots.
Boeing Co. also has stake in the outcome. American has said it will buy $6.5 billion worth of new Boeing airliners, but only if the pilots agree to a new contract.

If no accord is reached and APA strikes again, only Congress can send the pilots back to work, with a law to require them to accept the draft settlement proposed by the Presidential Emergency Board or to accept binding arbitration.
The terms of the offer the pilots are considering have been kept a close secret by both the union and American, and it was not known how they compared with the PEB's recommendations.

The board backed a 6.5 percent pay raise for the pilots, along with concessionary terms for stock options. The airline's last pay offer was 6.5 percent. The union wanted 11 percent to cover its last three years without a pay increase and for the next four.
The PEB did not agree to an APA demand that its pilots fly the small regional jets American is to buy for its American Eagle commuter line, but did suggest some job security concessions.
American wants the planes to be flown by its Eagle pilots, who are paid an average of $35,000 a year and belong to a different union, against $120,000 for American's APA pilots.

The union has said it feared American would gradually move the smaller Eagle jets, which have a range of up to 2,000 miles, onto routes now flown by American's bigger jets, and reap the benefits of lower wages at the expense of APA jobs.
To give APA added job security, the PEB recommended that American agree to limits on the number of its regional jets it operates, the routes they fly and the airports they serve.
